title: Given an array of numbers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, where the chosen elements keep their original order but need not be contiguous. Explain the quadratic dynamic programming and the optimal patience-sorting approach, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence (Longest Strictly Rising Pick)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Increasing Subsequence finds the longest subsequence whose values strictly increase while preserving the original order. The quadratic dynamic programming defines the best length ending at each index as one plus the best among all earlier smaller elements. The optimal approach maintains the smallest possible tail for each achievable length using binary search, giving n log n time.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India reviews a customer's monthly closing balances and wants the longest run of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, as a signal of improving financial health.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep the smallest tail for each length and binary-search each element into place for n log n.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Increasing Subsequence finds the longest subsequence whose values strictly increase while preserving the original order. The quadratic dynamic programming defines the best length ending at each index as one plus the best among all earlier smaller elements. The optimal approach maintains the smallest possible tail for each achievable length using binary search, giving n log n time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India reviews a customer's monthly closing balances and wants the longest run of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, as a signal of improving financial health.

**One line to remember:** Keep the smallest tail for each length and binary-search each element into place for n log n.

sections.s2_technical:
The quadratic version keeps an array where the entry at index i is the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending exactly at i. For each i we look back at every earlier index j, and if the value at j is smaller than the value at i we can extend that subsequence, so we take one plus the best such length. The answer is the maximum entry. This is simple but costs order n squared.

The optimal version maintains a list of tails, where tails at position k is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k plus one: `for (int x : nums) { int pos = lowerBound(tails, x); if (pos == tails.size()) tails.add(x); else tails.set(pos, x); } return tails.size();`. A concrete check: with balances 10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18 the longest increasing run has length four, for example 2, 3, 7, 18. Senior nuance: the tails list is not itself a valid subsequence, only its length is meaningful; reconstructing the actual subsequence needs predecessor pointers, and the binary search gives n log n time with linear space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India analyses a customer's sequence of monthly closing balances and wants the longest stretch of months, not necessarily back to back, during which the balance strictly increased, as a measure of improving financial health for a credit decision. Checking every possible stretch is exponential. This is exactly how Longest Increasing Subsequence works: it finds the longest strictly rising pick in order.

The code defines a `FinancialHealthService` with `longestRisingRun(balances)` using the patience-sorting binary search. A `Demo` provides monthly balances and logs the longest rising run length.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is monthly balances ten, nine, two, five, three, seven, one hundred one, eighteen. Step 1: tails starts empty. Step 2: ten appends, tails is ten. Step 3: nine replaces ten at position zero because it is a smaller tail for length one, tails is nine. Step 4: two replaces nine, tails is two. Step 5: five appends, tails is two, five. Step 6: three replaces five at position one, tails is two, three. Step 7: seven appends, tails is two, three, seven. Step 8: one hundred one appends, tails is two, three, seven, one hundred one. Step 9: eighteen replaces one hundred one at position three, tails is two, three, seven, eighteen. The list length is four, so the longest strictly rising run has length four.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:42:05 PM com.bank.finhealth.service.FinancialHealthService longestRisingRun
INFO: Longest strictly rising run = 4
Oct 27, 2026 9:42:05 PM com.bank.finhealth.FinancialHealthApplication main
INFO: Final rising-run length = 4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Increasing Subsequence asks for the longest strictly rising pick of elements while keeping their original order, and I always present two solutions to show depth. The straightforward dynamic programming keeps, for each index, the length of the best increasing subsequence ending there, computed by looking back at every earlier smaller element and extending it, which is clear but costs quadratic time.

The optimal approach is patience sorting with binary search. I maintain a list of tails where the entry at each position holds the smallest possible ending value of an increasing subsequence of that length. For each new element I binary-search for the first tail that is greater than or equal to it; if none exists the element extends the longest run and I append it, otherwise I overwrite that tail because this element gives a smaller, more extendable ending for that length. The length of the tails list is the answer, and I am careful to note that the tails list itself is not a valid subsequence, only its length is meaningful, so reconstructing the actual sequence needs predecessor pointers.

At the National Bank of India I used this on a customer's monthly closing balances to find the longest stretch of strictly rising balances as a credit-health signal. I ran the n log n version so it stayed fast even over long balance histories pulled from the warehouse. Explaining the quadratic dynamic programming, the smallest-tail insight behind the n log n method, and the subtlety that the tails array encodes only the length are exactly what convince an interviewer I understand this problem beyond a memorised template.
